method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe hypertension needs urgent consultation; hypertension with encephalopathy is a medical emergency.** All childhood hypertension needs monitoring and follow-up.
claims.source_text: Severe hypertension requires urgent consultation and management. Hypertension associated with encephalopathy is a medical emergency … All hypertension in children requires monitoring and follow-up
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Measure BP annually in healthy children.** Confirm an abnormal machine reading, preferably manually, with a correctly sized cuff.
claims.source_text: Blood pressure should be measured annually in healthy children … Where possible, abnormal machine BP measurement should be confirmed, preferably with a manual BP, ensuring appropriately sized cuff is used for accurate measurement
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Scope: ages 1–17 years, not infants.** Childhood hypertension predicts adult hypertension, cardiovascular disease and end-organ damage.
claims.source_text: This guideline will focus on the paediatric population aged 1–17 years (not infants) … Hypertension in childhood is a key predictor of risk for hypertension, cardiovascular disease and end organ damage in adulthood
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Over 6 years: mostly primary**, linked to obesity or family history. **Under 6 years: secondary is more common**, mostly renal, with greater risk of hypertensive emergency.
claims.source_text: Primary/essential hypertension accounts for the majority of hypertension in children >6 years old and is generally associated with obesity or a family history of hypertension … Secondary hypertension is more common in younger children (<6 years old) with renal disease being the most prevalent cause. This population is at greater risk of hypertensive emergencies due to an underlying condition
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors:** overweight/obesity · male sex · family history · low birth weight/IUGR · prematurity · excess salt · inactivity · chronic disease such as CKD or diabetes.
claims.source_text: Overweight/obesity Male sex Family history of hypertension Low birth weight/intrauterine growth restriction Prematurity Excess dietary salt intake Physical inactivity Chronic health concerns, eg chronic kidney disease, diabetes
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Red-flag history:** headache/vomiting · blurred vision · altered mental state · seizures · chest pain/palpitations · breathlessness · cardiac failure · past AKI.
claims.source_text: Headache/vomiting Blurred vision Change in mental state Seizures Chest pain/palpitations Shortness of breath Cardiac failure Past history of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine:** confirm the BP · tachycardia and **four-limb BP** for upper/lower discrepancy · height and weight · end-organ damage (retinopathy, apical heave, hepatomegaly, oedema, palpable kidneys, facial nerve palsy).
claims.source_text: Confirm hypertension (See measuring blood pressure section below) Vitals: tachycardia, four limb BP for upper and lower limb discrepancy Height and weight: obesity, growth retardation Signs of end organ damage Fundoscopy: hypertensive retinopathy Cardiovascular: apical heave, hepatomegaly, oedema Chronic renal failure: palpable kidneys Focal neurology eg facial nerve palsies
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Use the correct cuff, erring larger** — a small cuff creates artificial hypertension. **Cuff width = 40% of the upper-arm length** (shoulder tip to elbow).
claims.source_text: Ensure the correct cuff size is selected for each patient, favouring a larger rather than smaller cuff (smaller cuff creates artificial hypertension) BP cuff width should be 40% of the length of the arm measure from the shoulder tip to the elbow
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check any abnormal oscillometric reading with a manual BP.**
claims.source_text: Abnormal oscillatory BP measurement needs checking with a manual BP from the child's arm
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Normal:** under the 90th centile (1–13 years); under 120/80 mmHg (13–17 years). **Elevated:** 90th to under 95th centile, or 120/80 to under the 95th centile, whichever is lower (1–13 years); 120/<80 to 129/<80 mmHg (13–17 years).
claims.source_text: For children aged 1 to 13 years For children aged 13-17 years Normal blood pressure <90th centile <120/<80 mmHg Elevated blood pressure ≥90th centile to <95th centile or 120/80 mmHg to <95th centile (whichever is lower) 120/<80 to 129/<80 mmHg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stage 1:** 95th centile to under 95th + 12 mmHg, or 130/80–139/89, whichever is lower (1–13 years); 130/80–139/89 mmHg (13–17 years).
claims.source_text: For children aged 1 to 13 years For children aged 13-17 years … Stage 1 Hypertension ≥95th centile to <95th centile + 12 mmHg or 130/80 to 139/89 mmHg (whichever is lower) 130/80 to 139/89 mmHg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stage 2:** 95th centile + 12 mmHg or more, or 140/90 or more, whichever is lower (1–13 years); 140/90 mmHg or more (13–17 years).
claims.source_text: For children aged 1 to 13 years For children aged 13-17 years … Stage 2 Hypertension ≥95th centile + 12 mmHg, or ≥140/90 mmHg (whichever is lower) ≥140/90 mmHg
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hypertensive urgency:** over the 95th centile + 30 mmHg (1–13 years) or over 180/120 (13–17 years) **without** end-organ symptoms or signs.
claims.source_text: For children aged 1 to 13 years For children aged 13-17 years … Hypertensive Urgency >95th centile + 30 mmHg without symptoms/signs of target end organ damage (See Examination) >180/120 without symptoms/signs of target end organ damage (See Examination)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hypertensive emergency:** the same thresholds **with encephalopathy** — headache, vomiting, vision change, facial nerve palsy, lethargy, seizures, coma — ± end-organ damage.
claims.source_text: Hypertensive Emergency >95th centile + 30 mmHg associated with encephalopathy, eg headache vomiting, vision changes and neurological symptoms (facial nerve palsy, lethargy, seizures, coma) +/- target-end organ damage >180/120 associated with encephalopathy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe hypertension: discuss with the renal team and retrieval/ICU team.**
claims.source_text: Emergency management of severe hypertension Discuss with renal team and retrieval/ICU team
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urgency, if medically stable:** a short-acting oral agent while investigating — **nifedipine 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day (max 20 mg), titrated to a maximum of 3 mg/kg/day (max 120 mg).**
claims.source_text: Hypertensive urgency If medically stable, consider short acting oral agents while investigating cause Nifedipine Commence 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day (max 20 mg) and titrate up as required to a maximum of 3 mg/kg/day (max 120 mg)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Emergency: IV therapy with renal and retrieval/ICU input. Lower BP gradually — by 25% of the original value every 24 hours** — towards the estimated 95th centile; slow down if symptoms develop.
claims.source_text: Hypertensive emergency Intravenous therapy; discuss with renal team and retrieval/ICU team Aim to gradually reduce BP to the patient's estimated 95th centile Decrease BP by 25% of the original value every 24 hours till target BP reached. Reduce rate of decrease if patient becomes symptomatic
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First-line:** UEC, CMP, urinalysis ± renal ultrasound. **Consider** LFT, HbA1c and fasting lipids, especially if BMI is over the 95th centile.
claims.source_text: First-line investigations UEC, CMP, urinalysis +/- renal ultrasound Consider LFT, Hb1Ac, fasting lipids particularly in children with BMI >95th centile
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Further tests only with a general or renal paediatrician**, if under 6 years, secondary cause suspected, or first-line tests abnormal: FBE, bicarbonate, renin/aldosterone, TFT, metanephrines, cortisol, fasting glucose; urine microscopy, protein/creatinine ratio, catecholamines, drug screen; renal Doppler, DMSA, CTA/MRA; echo, sleep study.
claims.source_text: Further investigations should only be considered in consultation with a general or renal paediatrician Consider further testing if child meets one of the following criteria: <6 years Concerns for secondary causes on history/examination Abnormal first-line investigations Further Investigations Bloods: FBE, Bicarbonate, renin/aldosterone ratio, TFT, plasma metanephrins, cortisol, fasting glucose Urine: microscopy, protein/creatinine ratio, catecholamines, drug screen Imaging: renal doppler ultrasound, DMSA, CTA/MRA Other: echocardiogram, sleep study
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lifestyle:** diet rich in fruit, vegetables, legumes, fish, poultry, lean meat and low-fat dairy; limit high-sodium, fatty and sugary foods; **40 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise 3–5 days a week**; consider behavioural support for weight.
claims.source_text: Rich in fresh fruit and vegetables/legumes, fish, poultry, lean red meat and low fat dairy Limit intake of high sodium, fat or sugar containing foods Lifestyle modifications Increase physical activity, aiming 40 minutes moderate to vigorous exercise 3-5 days/week Consider counselling/behavioural techniques to help address weight management and metabolic risk
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start medicines if:** conservative measures fail · symptomatic hypertension · stage 2 with no modifiable risk factor · CKD or diabetes. **Only with a general or renal paediatrician.**
claims.source_text: Should be commenced if: Conservative measures have failed Symptomatic hypertension develops Stage 2 hypertension with no modifiable risk factors Hypertension in setting of chronic kidney disease/diabetes Medical management should only be commenced in consultation with a general or renal paediatrician
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First line: a long-acting calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine.** Other agents may be preferred with BMI over the 95th centile, diabetes or proteinuria.
claims.source_text: Long-acting calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine are recommended as first line therapy. Other medication may be preferred in children with BMI >95th centile, diabetes or proteinuria
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the local paediatric team** for red flags or ongoing concern, hypertensive urgency or emergency, or when medical treatment is needed. Children **without severe features can be discharged** with follow-up.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when Red flags (see history section above) or ongoing concerns are present Hypertensive urgency or hypertensive emergency Medical management of hypertension is required … Hypertensive children without severe features may be discharged with appropriate follow-up
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hypertension in children and adolescents' (Last updated June 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypertension_in_children_and_adolescents/, retrieved 2026-09-23
